body:
The Shakti Peetha tradition

Shaktism is the religious tradition centred on the worship of Shakti, the Divine Mother. A Shakti Peetha is a sacred place particularly associated with the goddess.

According to a widespread religious narrative, places where parts of the body or ornaments of Sati fell became sacred seats of the goddess. A commonly followed tradition identifies 51 Shakti Peethas, although their precise number and geographical lists vary across texts and religious traditions.

Location and identity of Ambaji

Ambaji is situated in Danta taluka of Banaskantha district, close to the Gujarat-Rajasthan border. It lies in the Arasur region of the Aravalli hills.

The principal religious institution is the Arasuri Ambaji Temple. Ambaji is recognised as one of the important Shakti Peethas and is associated in religious tradition with the heart of Sati.

Distinctive form of worship

A particularly important feature of Ambaji Temple is the absence of a conventional anthropomorphic idol of the principal goddess in the sanctum.

Instead, worship is centred on the sacred Shree Visa Yantra. A yantra is a symbolic geometric representation of divine power used in religious worship. The yantra is adorned according to the temple's ritual tradition.

The principal object of worship at Ambaji Temple is the sacred Visa Yantra rather than a conventional human-shaped idol of the goddess.

Gabbar Hill

Gabbar Hill, located approximately 4 km west of Ambaji town, is traditionally regarded as the original sacred seat of the goddess.

An important feature of the hilltop shrine is its continuously burning sacred lamp. Pilgrims visit both the main Ambaji Temple and Gabbar Hill, making the surrounding landscape an integral part of the pilgrimage.

Bhadarvi Poonam pilgrimage

The annual Bhadarvi Poonam gathering is particularly associated with Ambaji. It takes place around the full-moon day of the Hindu lunar month of Bhadrapada.

Groups of devotees traditionally undertake journeys on foot to Ambaji from different parts of Gujarat and neighbouring regions. The pilgrimage illustrates the importance of religious routes as well as the destination itself.

Navratri is also significant at Ambaji because of its association with worship of the Divine Mother.

Ambaji and Pavagadh

Ambaji and Pavagadh are both important centres of Shakti worship, but they have different geographical and religious identities. Ambaji is situated in the Aravalli region of northern Gujarat and is particularly associated with the Visa Yantra and Gabbar Hill. Pavagadh is situated in Panchmahal district and is associated with Kalika Mata and the historic Champaner-Pavagadh complex.

Prelims focus

  • Ambaji is situated in Danta taluka of Banaskantha district.
  • Arasuri Ambaji is associated with the Shakti Peetha tradition.
  • According to religious tradition, the heart of Sati is associated with Ambaji.
  • The principal object of worship is the Shree Visa Yantra.
  • Gabbar Hill is regarded as the original sacred seat of the goddess.
  • Bhadarvi Poonam is the distinctive annual pilgrimage gathering.

[References: District Banaskantha, Government of Gujarat, Ambaji Temple and Gabbar Hill, Ambaji; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook, Banas Kantha, Part XII-A, District Highlights and Ambaji Gabbar motif; Gujarat Tourism, Ambaji Temple; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Gabbar Hill, about 4 km west of Ambaji, has a sacred lamp; the town’s Arasuri Ambaji Temple centres worship on the Shree Visa Yantra.
pictures.caption: Ambaji Temple and Gabbar Hill.

title: Ambaji: Arasuri Shakti Peetha and Gabbar Hill

body:
Jain pilgrimage and Tirthankaras

Jainism recognises 24 Tirthankaras in the present traditional cycle of time. A Tirthankara is a spiritual teacher who shows the path towards liberation from the cycle of birth and death.

Places associated with the lives, teachings, spiritual achievements or liberation of Tirthankaras have particular significance in Jain pilgrimage.

Location and religious importance of Palitana

Palitana is situated in Bhavnagar district in the Saurashtra region. Its religious importance arises primarily from the Jain temple complex on Shatrunjaya Hill, also written as Shatrunjay.

Shatrunjaya is particularly sacred to the Shvetambara Jain tradition. Its principal religious association is with Adinatha, also known as Rishabhanatha or Rishabha, the first Tirthankara.

According to Jain tradition, Adinatha preached and meditated at Shatrunjaya. These associations distinguish Palitana from Girnar, which is principally associated with the liberation of the 22nd Tirthankara, Neminatha.

Temple architecture and organisation

The temples of Shatrunjaya were developed over several centuries, with major construction and reconstruction occurring from the medieval period onwards. The complex contains hundreds of shrines rather than a single temple.

Many temples feature intricately carved stone and marble, pillared halls, courtyards, sanctums and numerous shikharas.

The temples are organised into groups called tunks or tuks. Each tunk is an enclosure containing a principal temple and smaller associated shrines. This arrangement creates a large temple complex adapted to the hilltop terrain.

  • Adinatha Temple: The principal shrine associated with the first Tirthankara.
  • Chaumukh Temple: A four-faced shrine built in 1618 CE, with images of Adinatha facing the 4 cardinal directions.
  • Angar Pir Shrine: A shrine associated with a Muslim saint within the wider sacred landscape of Shatrunjaya.

Pilgrimage practices

The ascent of Shatrunjaya Hill is itself an important devotional activity. Pilgrims climb the stone stairways, visit the shrines and undertake religious observances.

Kartik Purnima is especially important because it marks the conclusion of Chaturmas, the traditional 4-month period of religious observance associated with the rainy season. It marks the reopening of the principal pilgrimage season at Shatrunjaya.

The religious observance of the hill illustrates the relationship between Jain spiritual discipline, pilgrimage and the natural environment.

Prelims focus

  • Palitana is situated in Bhavnagar district.
  • Its Jain temples are located on Shatrunjaya Hill.
  • Adinatha or Rishabhanatha is the first Tirthankara.
  • Tunks are enclosures containing groups of Jain temples.
  • Kartik Purnima marks the conclusion of Chaturmas and the reopening of the pilgrimage season.
  • Trap: Palitana is principally associated with Adinatha, whereas Girnar is principally associated with Neminatha.

[References: NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Chapter 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, pp. 88–89; NCERT, Class 11, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 94–95; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 10, Social Science, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6, pp. 49–50; Gujarat Tourism, Palitana and Shatrunjaya Hill; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Palitana and Shatrunjaya Hill; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Pilgrims ascending Shatrunjaya Hill.

title: Palitana: Shatrunjaya Hill and the Jain Temple Complex

body:
Location and character of Girnar

Girnar is a group of sacred mountains situated near Junagadh in Junagadh district. It is also known historically and traditionally as Revatak Parvata or Girinagar.

Unlike a pilgrimage centre organised primarily around one religious shrine, Girnar contains several important religious sites distributed across its foothills, slopes and peaks. It is particularly sacred to both Hindus and Jains.

Girnar in Jain tradition

The principal Jain religious association of Girnar is with Neminatha, also called Arishtanemi, the 22nd Tirthankara.

According to Jain tradition, Neminatha undertook spiritual practices and attained liberation, or moksha, on Girnar. The mountain therefore holds special significance as a place associated with his spiritual achievements.

The historic Jain temple complex contains several important shrines, including the temples associated with Neminatha, Mallinatha and Samprati Raja. The principal Neminatha Temple is one of the prominent religious buildings of the complex.

Shatrunjaya at Palitana is primarily associated with Adinatha, the first Tirthankara. Girnar is primarily associated with Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara.

Girnar in Hindu tradition

  • Amba Mata Temple: An important hill shrine dedicated to the Divine Mother.
  • Gorakhnath: A sacred peak associated with the Nath tradition and the yogi Gorakhnath.
  • Dattatreya shrine: A sacred summit associated with Guru Dattatreya.
  • Bhavnath Mahadev Temple: A Shiva shrine located at the foothills, known as Girnar Taleti.
  • Damodar Kund: A sacred water body near the foothills associated with Hindu religious rites.

Lili Parikrama

The annual Lili Parikrama is a religious circumambulation around the Girnar mountain landscape. Parikrama means the ritual movement around a sacred object, shrine or geographical feature.

The traditional observance takes place from Kartik Shukla Ekadashi, the 11th day of the bright lunar fortnight, to Kartik Purnima, its full-moon day.

The pilgrimage begins in the vicinity of Bhavnath Mahadev Temple and follows a route around the mountain through the surrounding natural landscape.

Lili Parikrama is different from climbing Girnar to worship at its summit shrines. The former is a circumambulation around the mountain, while the latter is an ascent to religious sites on the hill.

Bhavnath Mahadev Fair

The Bhavnath Mahadev Fair is associated with Mahashivratri and takes place at Girnar Taleti. It attracts Shiva devotees, ascetics and members of religious orders, including Naga sadhus.

The fair is associated with worship at Bhavnath Mahadev Temple and religious observances connected with Mrigi Kund.

Associated historical heritage

The Junagadh-Girnar region also contains Ashoka's rock edicts and Buddhist archaeological remains, including the Khapra Kodiya caves and the Intwa monastery site. These remains demonstrate the long historical development of the region's religious and cultural heritage.

Prelims focus

  • Girnar is situated in Junagadh district and is also associated with the name Revatak Parvata.
  • Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara, is traditionally associated with liberation at Girnar.
  • Amba Mata, Gorakhnath and Dattatreya are important Hindu associations.
  • Bhavnath Mahadev Fair is associated with Mahashivratri.
  • Lili Parikrama takes place between Kartik Shukla Ekadashi and Kartik Purnima.
  • Trap: Lili Parikrama is a circumambulation around the mountain, not simply a climb to its summit.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 10, Social Science, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6, Places of Indian Cultural Heritage, pp. 49–50; District Junagadh, Government of Gujarat, Girnar; Gujarat Tourism, Girnar Hill and Bhavnath Mahadev Fair; Ministry of Tourism, Utsav, Girnar Lili Parikrama; Girinagar: Junagadh and Mount Girnar, Chapter 24, Dev-kot and Nearby Jain Shrines at Girnar; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Girnar’s sites grouped by foothills, hill shrines and sacred peaks, with ascent distinguished from Lili Parikrama around the mountain.
pictures.caption: Girnar's sacred sites and pilgrimage traditions.

title: Girnar: Neminatha, Hindu Shrines and Lili Parikrama

body:
Location and religious significance

Pavagadh is a prominent hill situated near Halol in Panchmahal district of Gujarat. The Kalika Mata Temple on its summit is an important centre of Shakti worship.

Kalika Mata is revered as the guardian goddess of the hill. The temple attracts pilgrims throughout the year and is particularly important during Navratri.

Pavagadh is traditionally recognised as a Shakti Peetha. Its principal religious association with Kalika Mata distinguishes it from Ambaji, where the main shrine is dedicated to Arasuri Ambaji and worship is centred on the Visa Yantra.

Relationship between Champaner and Pavagadh

Champaner is the historic settlement situated at the foot of Pavagadh Hill. Together, Champaner and Pavagadh preserve the remains of several historical periods and religious traditions.

  • Pavagadh Hill: Contains the historic hill fortress, religious shrines and the living pilgrimage tradition centred on Kalika Mata.
  • Champaner: Contains the remains of a former capital of the Gujarat Sultanate, including mosques, palaces, residential structures and water-management installations.

Sultan Mahmud Begada captured Pavagadh in 1484 and developed Champaner as his capital. The settlement continued as the capital of Gujarat until 1536.

The Jama Masjid of Champaner is particularly important for its architectural integration of regional Indian and Islamic building traditions.

UNESCO World Heritage recognition

The Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2004 as a cultural property under criteria (iii), (iv), (v) and (vi).

The recognised property includes prehistoric remains, fortifications, religious buildings, the historic pre-Mughal capital, water-management structures and the continuing religious tradition of Pavagadh.

Its significance arises from the combined historical, architectural and religious features of the landscape, rather than from a single building.

The UNESCO World Heritage property is the Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park as a whole. The Kalika Mata Temple is an important living religious component of that property, not a separately inscribed World Heritage property.

A multi-faith cultural landscape

The region contains Hindu shrines, Jain temples and Islamic religious architecture. These buildings reflect the presence and development of different religious communities over successive historical periods.

The site is also an example of the coexistence of archaeological heritage and living religious heritage. Much of the former capital survives as archaeological remains, while Kalika Mata Temple continues to function as an active place of pilgrimage.

Prelims focus

  • Pavagadh is located near Halol in Panchmahal district.
  • Its principal pilgrimage shrine is dedicated to Kalika Mata.
  • Mahmud Begada captured Pavagadh in 1484.
  • Champaner remained the capital of Gujarat until 1536.
  • Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park received UNESCO World Heritage recognition in 2004.
  • Trap: The UNESCO inscription applies to the complete archaeological park, not only the Kalika Mata Temple.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Class 10, Social Science, English medium, 2020 reprint, Chapter 6, Places of Indian Cultural Heritage; District Panchmahal, Government of Gujarat, Pavagadh; Gujarat Tourism, Kalika Mata Temple and Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park, List No. 1101, inscription of 2004, Outstanding Universal Value and criteria (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), listed as a cultural World Heritage property at the consultation cutoff of 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Pavagadh Hill, its living Kalika Mata pilgrimage shrine, and Champaner at its foot form one UNESCO cultural World Heritage property, inscribed in 2004.

title: Pavagadh: Kalika Mata and the Champaner World Heritage Landscape
